name: Umar Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Umar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm goes at half five, and I'm on the minibus by half six with the rest of the framing gang. We're putting up council flats on Station Road for a big contractor, four storeys, timber frame on a concrete base. I'm what they call an improver, so I carry, I cut what Gary marks out, I fix noggins and I sweep up more than I'd like. Gary's been a chippy for thirty years and he's the reason I'm still there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that at the end of the week there's a floor where there wasn't one, and people are going to live in it, families off the waiting list. What wears me out is the cold in the mornings and getting shouted at when I've cut something an inch short, which still happens. I left school at sixteen and did warehouse work for years, so this is the first job that feels like it's going somewhere. I'm slow, I know I'm slow, but I'm getting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying in the canteen for a year: told you so. The lads have been scaring each other with videos of robot dogs, and I never believed any of it. I'd probably say it at the union branch meeting too, that we wasted a lot of breath on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I get to keep learning my trade the slow way, which is the only way I know. Nobody makes me use an app I don't understand. Gary retires in a few years and maybe I'm the one marking out by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes, so I'd keep turning up and keep putting a bit away each month, like now. I want to finish my NVQ, that's the trade qualification, by the end of next year. Nadia and I talked about a cheap holiday, so maybe we'd finally book it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. It's like a storm that was on the forecast and then just didn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody makes you use an app. Is that something you worry about now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The site manager put the safety sign-in on a tablet last month and I stood there like an idiot while a lad half my age did it for me. I don't have AI on my phone and I don't want it. In this picture I can just carry on doing it with a pencil behind my ear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Nadia say if you came home and told her this was how it turned out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say good, now stop reading the news in bed. She's a care worker, so she was never worried about a robot washing old Mrs Patel, she says that's a fantasy. She'd want us to start looking at a bigger flat.

S0.say: I'd tell the lads in the canteen and the union branch that I always said it was hype. We wasted a lot of breath worrying about robot videos.
S0.think: Privately it means I get to learn my trade slowly, the only way I know, without being pushed onto apps. Maybe I take over marking out when Gary retires.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving a bit each month as he does now. Aims to finish his NVQ by the end of next year and finally book a cheap holiday with his partner Nadia.
S0.feel: Relieved, like a forecast storm that never came.
S0.quote: I don't have AI on my phone and I don't want it. In this picture I can just carry on doing it with a pencil behind my ear.
S0.fieldNote: Umar is proud of being a late starter who has finally found a trade with a future. His resistance to technology is personal and a bit embarrassed: the tablet sign-in story stung. In the calm picture his whole plan is simply the slow apprenticeship he already has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the union has to get in early and make sure it's done with us, not to us. Online I'd share stuff about protecting workers, I always do. I'd say it's the bosses who'll save money and we're the ones who'll have to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared I'm the one who gets left behind. Gary will be fine, he's nearly done, and the young lads pick up tech like breathing. Me, I'm the improver who still can't work the sign-in tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd go to the branch rep and ask what training they're pushing for, because I wouldn't know where to start on my own. I'd keep putting the same bit away, maybe a bit more, so we've got three or four months of rent if work goes quiet. I'd stay put and see what the company actually brings in before I panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not the end of the world, but like being the last one picked for a team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your job do you picture changing first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cutting, probably. There's already a machine at the yard that cuts the studs to length from a drawing, and the gaffer says one day it'll do the whole frame panel. If that comes to site, the job I do now, carrying and cutting to Gary's marks, is exactly the bit that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see, but you also said you're scared of being left behind. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, fair. I suppose waiting is what I do when I'm scared. It's not clever, but it's honest. I'd lean on the union because I trust them more than I trust myself with this stuff.

S1.say: I'd say at work and online that the union has to get in early so change is done with workers, not to them. The bosses save the money and we do the changing.
S1.think: Privately he fears he's the one left behind: the old hands are nearly done and the young lads pick up tech easily. He still can't work the site sign-in tablet.
S1.do: Asks the union rep what training they're pushing for and puts a bit more aside to reach three or four months of rent. Stays in the job and waits to see what the company brings in.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like being the last one picked for a team.
S1.quote: I suppose waiting is what I do when I'm scared. It's not clever, but it's honest.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is political and collective; his private line is a personal fear of being the slowest learner. He names his own habit of freezing when anxious, which was striking. The stud-cutting machine at the yard is his concrete picture of what goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be angry, and I'd say so. Online I'd be sharing every petition going, saying the government has to stop firms laying people off for machines. At work I'd be saying we should all walk out before they bring the first one on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is nothing. I'd be about twenty-nine, half trained, with no school certificates and no idea how to use any of it. I think I'd be one of the first out the gate, and so would Gary even though he's the best chippy I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. Keep in mind there are only about 2 years before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent, food and the bus pass, and try to get from three months saved to six. I'd go to every union meeting and march if there's a march, because I think the only thing that slows this is people standing together. Once it arrives I honestly don't know. I'd probably end up claiming whatever help there is and leaning on Nadia's wage while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like the floor I've been building is being pulled out from under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, is there anything you'd try to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People will say learn the robots, but who's going to teach a slow learner like me in two years? I'd maybe finish the NVQ just so I've got one piece of paper. But I don't believe a certificate in carpentry is worth much once a machine does carpentry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nadia the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm sorry, because we were finally planning things. Then I'd say at least yours is a caring job, and she'd laugh and say the robots are coming for that too. I think we'd sit there and work out how long the savings last, on the back of the gas bill.

S2.say: I'd say loudly that the government has to stop firms laying people off for machines. I'd share every petition and say we should walk out before the first robot comes on site.
S2.think: Two years is nothing for someone half trained with no school certificates. He expects to be among the first let go, along with even the best chippies he knows.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent, food and travel to stretch savings from three months towards six. Goes to every union meeting and protest, then expects to rely on state help and his partner's wage once it arrives.
S2.feel: Sick, as if the floor he has been building is being pulled out from under him.
S2.quote: I don't believe a certificate in carpentry is worth much once a machine does carpentry.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture turns his politics into anger and his plans into survival maths. He doesn't believe he can retrain in time and says so plainly. The image of working out the savings on the back of the gas bill came out without any prompting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before really, I'd want the union and the government on it, pushing for rules on how fast firms can bring robots onto sites. Five years is long enough to make proper laws, so I'd be saying there's no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at thirty-two, maybe a proper chippy by then. That's the cruel bit, I'd just be getting good at it when it stops mattering. But it gives me time I didn't have in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 5 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the NVQ in the first year, no matter what. Then I'd ask the branch about the courses they keep mentioning, maybe something like site safety supervision, because someone will have to watch the machines and sign things off. I'd keep saving, aim for six months, and I'd try to get on the union committee so I hear things early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the kind where you can still do something. Less sick than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools. Would five years of warning change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the union ran a class and Gary went with me, I'd sit at the back and try. I won't do it on my own off some video. I need someone in the room who doesn't make me feel thick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra years that you couldn't do in the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plan with Nadia properly instead of panicking. We could decide whether we stay in the city where the work is or go back near her mum. In the fast one there's no deciding, things just happen to you.

S3.say: I'd say the union and the government must use the five years to make proper rules on how fast firms can bring robots onto sites. There's no excuse with that much warning.
S3.think: He'd be about thirty-two and finally a proper chippy just as it stops mattering. Still, it gives him time he didn't have in the fast picture.
S3.do: Finishes his NVQ in the first year, then asks the union about courses such as site safety supervision. Keeps saving towards six months and tries to join the union committee to hear news early.
S3.feel: Anxious, but able to act, and less sick than with two years.
S3.quote: That's the cruel bit, I'd just be getting good at it when it stops mattering.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time makes him willing to consider learning, but only in a group with someone he trusts beside him. His sense of injustice centres on timing: he started late and will peak just as the trade empties. He sees the union as both shield and classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a fair deal, so the country should plan it like it planned the mines closing, only better this time. Online I'd be pushing for retraining money and shorter weeks so people keep some work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels like a long way off, and I know myself, I'd probably put it off for the first few. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, and I'd like to be a foreman by then, or something like that. Part of me thinks I'd still be finished, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 10 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, honestly, I'd keep going on site and finish the NVQ, that's the plan anyway. I'd save a bit more and stay active in the branch, because ten years is long enough to win something if enough of us push. Maybe around year five I'd look at what jobs are left and train for one, but I can't see that far ahead today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared, because it's far away. But it sits there in the background, like a letter you haven't opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put it off. What do you think would finally make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it on our own site. When the first robot frames a wall on Station Road or wherever we are, I'd move. Until I see it with my own eyes it's just men in suits on telly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would anything change for you and Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We might go ahead and have a kid, which we wouldn't in the two-year one. Ten years is a whole childhood nearly. I'd want to know there's some kind of safety net by then, though, or I'd feel like I was being careless.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for a fair deal, planned better than the mine closures were. Online I'd push for retraining money and shorter working weeks.
S4.think: Privately he admits he'd put off acting for the first few years because it feels far away. He'd be thirty-seven and part of him thinks he'd still be finished, just later.
S4.do: Keeps working on site, finishes the NVQ and saves a little more while staying active in his union branch. Plans to look at retraining around year five, once he sees robots on his own site.
S4.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, like an unopened letter sitting in the background.
S4.quote: Until I see it with my own eyes it's just men in suits on telly.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets him relax into his natural habit of waiting, and he knows it. The trigger for action is physical: a robot framing a wall on his own site. The long horizon even brings a child back into his plans with Nadia, as long as there's a safety net.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. I'd be half trained with nothing else to fall back on. What would help is the union having a real say, and the government paying people a proper wage while they retrain, with classes run by people who don't make you feel thick. Not an app, a person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. If a robot builds the flats cheaper, the council should get more flats, not the contractor a bigger profit. That's the bit I'd want someone to write down.

headlineQuote: If a robot builds the flats cheaper, the council should get more flats, not the contractor a bigger profit.
portrait: Umar Olsen is a 27-year-old improver on a timber-frame crew building council flats, who left school at sixteen and found carpentry late after years in warehouses. He lives with his partner Nadia, a care worker, and has a few months of rent saved. He is a committed union man who doesn't use AI and still feels embarrassed by the site's sign-in tablet. Calm if AI fizzles, he grows uneasy with steady change and alarmed by AGI in two years, when he expects to be among the first let go. More warning time makes him willing to learn, but only in a group, and he admits he'd wait until he saw a robot on his own site.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be half trained with nothing else to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A real say for the union, and government paying a proper wage during retraining, with classes taught in person by people who don't make him feel slow.
